I had to answer this one, even though I’ve never been to DTU, or to Denmark for that matter.

In short: absolutely yes. DTU’s ACT (Acoustic Technology) group is one of the largest acoustics research institutes in the world, and a very strong one. Add the fact that it sits close to Brüel & Kjær, the world’s largest maker of sound and vibration equipment, and DTU has an exceptionally rich acoustics culture.

  1. A giant: Finn Jacobsen

Sadly, he died far too young. If you’re interested in acoustic energy and how it flows, don’t miss Jacobsen: he published a great deal on sound intensity and particle velocity.

  • The book

I’ve strongly recommended this book in other answers too. Whether you’re new to acoustics or a seasoned researcher, it’s a classic for the ages. What sets it apart from most other introductory acoustics books is how carefully it works through the theory and how many examples it gives. I’ve long felt the urge to translate it into Chinese: there are very few acoustics books in Chinese, and even fewer translations. If any colleagues have read it and like it too, let’s think about translating it together.

  • Sound intensity

From the 1990s on, he devoted himself to sound intensity: active and reactive intensity, coherent and incoherent sound fields, particle velocity, near-field acoustic holography (NAH) and more.

  • Championing the Microflown particle velocity sensor

A picture first. Jacobsen appears on the cover page of one of the chapters of the Microflown e-book, which shows how much he did for the company. In its early days, Microflown used its particle velocity sensor mainly in research and hadn’t managed to commercialize it. For its first ten years the company worked closely with Professor Jacobsen, and it was he who proposed a complete calibration procedure for the sensor [3], which is what brought Microflown to market.

2. Compressive sensing + beamforming = compressive beamforming

Compressive sensing was introduced a little over a decade ago, but in acoustics it really took off after Angeliki Xenaki, then a PhD student at DTU, published Compressive beamforming [4] in 2014. She and Peter Gerstoft of the University of California, San Diego, then put out a flood of papers on compressive beamforming, many of them tied to ocean acoustics and of real practical value.

3. ACT’s other research areas

Architectural acoustics: Cheol-Ho Jeong, a confident Korean guy. I’ve heard him speak a few times, and he has a self-assurance you don’t often see in Asian researchers.

Beyond that, there’s structure-borne sound and electroacoustics (medical acoustics and hearing aids), which I don’t know well enough to comment on.

Oh, and they’ve recently made their mark in numerical acoustics too. The book that pulled the discontinuous Galerkin method together was written by a DTU professor, and they’ve been working together to bring this time-domain method, which allows flexible boundary conditions, into room acoustics. The building acoustics group at TU Eindhoven is working in the same direction.

I don’t know much about the job market in Denmark, but Copenhagen has B&K and the hearing aid maker GN ReSound (where Xenaki, mentioned above, used to work), so there should be plenty of opportunities. A DTU degree does, after all, guarantee a certain baseline of quality.

I’ve also just found out that Bang & Olufsen is in Copenhagen as well. It mainly makes audio equipment for consumer electronics, such as speakers for phones, TVs and computers. Bang & Olufsen has been around for 90 years, and its brand slogan is “a hallmark of Danish quality” [Wikipedia].
